honesty.note: Evidenced = Social Fetch sample (hand-tagged, directional, paraphrased, no usernames) or a primary NCAA rule. Inferred = our working hypothesis, not yet tested with families.

segments.name: 9th/10th Grade Planner
segments.who: Parent of a 9th or 10th grader. No coach has called. The risk is a paid service pitching a young athlete, and spending before the rules say anyone may reply.

plan.step: This month: read the by-grade checklist
plan.why: Problem #1 in the Social Fetch sample: 'just give me the steps'.

plan.step: Put the contact dates on your own calendar
plan.why: D1/D2 coaches generally cannot reply to you before the dates in the bylaws. Emailing earlier gets no answer by rule.

plan.step: Check every class against the NCAA-approved list
plan.why: Core-course mistakes cannot be fixed late.

plan.step: If you live in the Denver metro, check camps and trainers against their sources
plan.why: Every row shows its source and check date. Denver area only.

plan.step: Hold your money until a coach has actually written
plan.why: Spend nothing on showcases or services yet.

story.label: Perez: started in eighth grade and still found a home

segments.spend_note: Free path. Budget line to protect: nothing recurring before sophomore summer.

segments.name: Late-Start Junior/Senior Panic
segments.who: Junior or senior with no list, no film plan, no replies. Roster spots are filling. The risk is mass-emailing the wrong level and buying a panic service.

plan.step: Reset the level: D2, D3, NAIA and JUCO still fill rosters in senior year
plan.why: Chain 2 layer 3: aiming too high is the usual cause.

plan.step: Read the by-grade checklist for what is still open
plan.why: It tells you what is allowed now and what date comes next.

plan.step: Get your earliest contact dates, a 30-school target list and an athlete-voice email
plan.why: Coaches spot parent-written mail; a short, realistic list beats mass email.

plan.step: Open the Eligibility Center account if you have not
plan.why: Without it, no D1/D2 official visit.

story.label: Diego: junior college is a real first step

segments.spend_note: Spend only on verified essentials. One targeted camp, after a coach has replied.

segments.name: Burned by a Paid Recruiting Service or Showcase Circuit
segments.who: Family that paid a recruiting service or ran the showcase circuit and is asking 'was it worth it, and how do we cancel?' Parents in the sample report up to about $4K plus monthly fees.

plan.step: Check your athlete against sourced standards before paying anyone to judge level
plan.why: Chain 3: services did little families could not do; prices hidden until the end of the call.

plan.step: Compare what you bought with what is free
plan.why: Chain 3: services did little families could not do; prices hidden until the end of the call.

plan.step: Rebuild the timeline and tracker yourself
plan.why: The thing parents liked about services was the contact timeline.

plan.step: Spot the next pitch before it lands
plan.why: Red-flag checklist for sales calls and contracts.

plan.step: Redirect the remaining budget (view C)
plan.why: The $110 NCAA fee is the one cost every D1/D2 path needs.

story.label: Coward: zero D1 offers, a D3 start, a long climb

segments.spend_note: Cancellation terms vary by contract. Read yours; this site gives education, not legal advice.

segments.name: High-Academic D3 / Ivy / Merit-Aid Family
segments.who: Strong student, often swimming, tennis, lacrosse or golf. The questions are early-action with coach support and how athletic and academic aid stack.

plan.step: Lead with academic aid, then ask the coach about fit
plan.why: D3 gives no athletic scholarships; aid is academic or need-based.

plan.step: Do the roster and aid math before you fall for a school
plan.why: Know the spots and the real net cost.

plan.step: Check whether D3 offers athletic scholarships (it does not)
plan.why: Clears up the most common wrong assumption.

plan.step: Compare offers side by side before deadlines
plan.why: Early-decision commitments bind.

story.label: Marpet: no D1 offers? Division III can build an athlete

segments.spend_note: Highest household spend in the Aspen data ($100K+ band). Spend on visits that matter, not on volume.

segments.name: Clock/Mark Sport: Track, XC, Swim
segments.who: Athlete whose numbers are public. The lever is a verified mark at a meet coaches use, a clear list, and the right email, not a flashy video.

plan.step: Know the track dates and rules for your class year
plan.why: Track recruiting dates differ from team sports.

plan.step: Use the marks-to-roster playbook
plan.why: Turn a verified time into a target list.

plan.step: Check when track coaches may contact you
plan.why: Direct answer with the bylaw cited.

plan.step: Email in the athlete's voice with the mark in the subject
plan.why: Coaches skim; grad year and mark first.

story.label: Maya: her times were good, nobody knew yet

segments.spend_note: Aspen 2019 average for track is $191 and swimming $786, so the budget is modest. Protect it.

segments.name: Emerging Sport or JUCO/NAIA Transfer Path
segments.who: Girls' flag football, women's wrestling, or a family weighing JUCO then transfer. Few playbooks exist; the college pathway is new.

plan.step: Find your sport's pathway checklist
plan.why: Girls flag football, girls wrestling and boys volleyball are growing faster than most guides track.

plan.step: Read the JUCO-to-D1 path
plan.why: Many families use a JUCO year as a real first step.

plan.step: Learn the walk-on route where no scholarship exists yet
plan.why: New programs often fill through tryouts.

plan.step: Use the by-grade checklist and rule calendar
plan.why: Rules for new sports lag; confirm each date.

plan.step: See the full playbook shelf
plan.why: All sport and stage playbooks.

story.label: Rodriguez: stepped away? A new program can still find you

segments.spend_note: Cheap sports but a high information need. An emerging-sports program list is not on the site yet.

chains.title: Where do I start: give me the steps

layers.name: Stated complaint
layers.text: Parents say they don't know who/what/when/how and ask for a step list.

layers.name: Trigger
layers.text: A first recruiting video, camp invite, or a peer committing makes the family realize the process exists; often 8th-10th grade.
layers.source: v3/W7-segments/raw/ytc_ogjICDcgCro.json (class-of-2030 asks when to email); v3/W6-problems/PROBLEMS.md #5

layers.name: Underlying cause
layers.text: No neutral owner of the process: high school coach is not responsible, the NCAA publishes rules not plans, services sell rather than teach.

layers.name: What they tried
layers.text: Ask in TikTok comments, 'DM me', join FB groups, read blogs.

layers.name: Why it failed
layers.text: Answers are pitches or lead magnets; big FB groups ban school-specific questions; advice conflicts.

layers.name: Cost
layers.text: Time and missed windows (e.g. D1/D2 contact opens Jun 15 / Sep 1 after sophomore yr); risk of paying a service out of panic.

layers.name: Who else
layers.text: Athlete loses months of outreach; parent carries the stress; spouses disagree on spend.

layers.name: Job-to-be-done
layers.text: 'Tell me, for my kid's grade and sport, the 3 things to do this month.'

layers.name: Winning solution
layers.text: Free 'Start here by grade + sport' page that outputs a dated monthly checklist from the rule calendar, then routes to the Sport Pack.

layers.name: Proof it worked
layers.text: Parent can name this month's 3 tasks and the next contact date; checklist items ticked; first coach email sent within 14 days.

chains.title: Is it too late? Junior/senior with nothing

layers.name: Stated complaint
layers.text: 'My kid is a senior/junior and we have nothing. Is it too late?'

layers.name: Trigger
layers.text: Summer before senior year: teammates commit, D2 boards look full, a dream school goes silent.

layers.name: Underlying cause
layers.text: Started outreach late and aimed too high; never assessed realistic level.

layers.name: What they tried
layers.text: Mass-email, buy a service, post on X, attend late camps.

layers.name: Why it failed
layers.text: Wrong targets (P4/D1 boards filled by August), unanswered emails, no follow-up plan.

layers.name: Cost
layers.text: Eligibility of the window: roster spots filled; possible JUCO detour; money on panic services.

layers.name: Who else
layers.text: Athlete's confidence; club coaches; target coaches still filling the roster for next year.

layers.name: Job-to-be-done
layers.text: 'Find the programs still filling our class and get us in front of them before signing day.'

layers.name: Winning solution
layers.text: Senior-year sprint playbook: level reset to D2/D3/NAIA/JUCO, 30-school list, 4-touch follow-up cadence, 'we'll be in your area' visit email, JUCO/post-grad fallback.

layers.name: Proof it worked
layers.text: A coach reply or visit invite within 30 days; a roster spot or JUCO plan in hand by graduation.

chains.title: Is NCSA/a recruiting service worth it, and how do I cancel?

layers.name: Stated complaint
layers.text: Regret after paying; aggressive calls; can't cancel; 'is it worth it?'

layers.name: Trigger
layers.text: Unsolicited call/text from a service after a free profile or camp, often to a young athlete.

layers.name: Underlying cause
layers.text: Parents don't know what is free (NCAA rules, email, X) and fear their kid is invisible without paying.

layers.name: What they tried
layers.text: Sign up, sometimes at a 'discount'; ask groups.

layers.name: Why it failed
layers.text: Coaches dislike agency contact; services did nothing families couldn't do; prices hidden till end of call; refund refused under hardship.

layers.name: Cost
layers.text: Money: parents report up to ~$4K plus monthly fees; a contract during income loss.

layers.name: Who else
layers.text: Athlete (coaches ignore service emails); a minority report real offers, so families split.

layers.name: Job-to-be-done
layers.text: 'Get the organization and timeline a service gives, without the price or the sales pressure.'

layers.name: Winning solution
layers.text: Honest 'service vs DIY' comparison + cancel guide + the same timeline/tracker for a fixed low price.

layers.name: Proof it worked
layers.text: Family cancels or never signs; saves the fee; still sends weekly outreach from the tracker.

chains.title: What do I say to a coach, and on which channel?

layers.name: Stated complaint
layers.text: 'What do I actually write, and email vs X DM vs questionnaire?'

layers.name: Trigger
layers.text: First outreach push, or weeks of silence after the first emails.

layers.name: Underlying cause
layers.text: Emails written by parents, no grad year in subject, no film link, sent before contact dates.

layers.name: What they tried
layers.text: Random templates, mass DMs, creators' dead links.

layers.name: Why it failed
layers.text: Coaches skim and delete; D1/D2 can't reply before Jun 15/Sep 1 dates; silence read as rejection.

layers.name: Cost
layers.text: Time; a burned first impression with a target program.

layers.name: Who else
layers.text: Athlete must own it (coaches spot parent-written mail); target coaches flooded.

layers.name: Job-to-be-done
layers.text: 'Get a reply from the coaches who fit us.'

layers.name: Winning solution
layers.text: Sport-specific email/DM scripts written in the athlete's voice + follow-up cadence tied to the contact calendar.

layers.name: Proof it worked
layers.text: Reply rate per 10 emails sent; first coach reply.

chains.title: When can coaches contact us, and when should we start?

layers.name: Stated complaint
layers.text: 'When can coaches contact us, and when should we start?'

layers.name: Trigger
layers.text: Younger sibling or 8th-9th grader gets a service call; peers talk about offers.

layers.name: Underlying cause
layers.text: Rules differ by division and sport and change; most sources don't cite the bylaw.

layers.name: What they tried
layers.text: Ask creators; follow services' 'start freshman year' advice.

layers.name: Why it failed
layers.text: Conflicting advice; emailing D1 coaches early gets no reply by rule.

layers.name: Cost
layers.text: Wasted early spend; anxiety; or missed contact-opening dates.

layers.name: Who else
layers.text: Coaches bound by rules; athlete confused by silence.

layers.name: Job-to-be-done
layers.text: 'Know exactly what's allowed now and what date to act next.'

layers.name: Winning solution
layers.text: Bylaw-cited rule calendar by sport/division with date reminders.

layers.name: Proof it worked
layers.text: Parent acts on the opening date (e.g. Jun 15 after sophomore year) instead of guessing.

chains.title: How do I register with the NCAA / get the ID, and what does it cost?

layers.name: Stated complaint
layers.text: 'How do I get the NCAA ID? What does it cost?'

layers.name: Trigger
layers.text: A coach asks for the ID, or an official visit is scheduled.

layers.name: Underlying cause
layers.text: Confusion among NCAA ID, Eligibility Center Certification vs Profile account, fee, and NCSA.

layers.name: What they tried
layers.text: Ask creators and groups.

layers.name: Why it failed
layers.text: Mixed timing advice ('register sophomore year' vs 'don't apply yet').

layers.name: Cost
layers.text: Eligibility: no Certification account and transcripts means no D1/D2 official visit.

layers.name: Who else
layers.text: high school counselor (transcripts), college compliance, athlete.

layers.name: Job-to-be-done
layers.text: 'Make sure nothing on paper blocks my kid.'

layers.name: Winning solution
layers.text: Step-by-step Eligibility Center + NAIA registration walkthrough with fee and deadline.

layers.name: Proof it worked
layers.text: Account created, transcripts sent, official visit not blocked.

spending.source: Aspen Institute Project Play, National Youth Sports Parent Survey, 2024 (n=1,848, fielded Nov-Dec 2024)
